title: Week 104 · Lesson 128: Postpartum Care & Maternal Complications — FNP-Level Fourth-Trimester Safety
html:
PHASE 5 · FAMILY & LIFESPAN PRIMARY CARE

Week 104 — Lesson 128: Postpartum Care & Maternal Complications

FNP-level goal: Treat postpartum care as a longitudinal transition rather than a single six-week visit, recognize life-threatening complications through one year after pregnancy, assess physical recovery and mental health together, reconcile chronic disease and medications, and close the handoff from obstetric to primary care.

Learning Objectives

  • Organize postpartum care across early contact, ongoing assessment, and a comprehensive visit no later than 12 weeks, individualized to risk.
  • Differentiate expected recovery from hemorrhage, infection, hypertension, thromboembolism, cardiomyopathy, wound complications, and psychiatric emergency.
  • Assess mood, anxiety, sleep, substance use, safety, feeding, pelvic floor, sexual health, contraception, and chronic disease without fragmenting the patient.
  • Reconcile medications for postpartum physiology, lactation, kidney/liver function, and future pregnancy goals.
  • Create a durable primary-care transition for patients with preeclampsia, gestational diabetes, preterm birth, or other pregnancy complications.

Part 1 — The Fourth Trimester Is Not a Single Visit

ACOG describes postpartum care as an ongoing process, with contact within the first three weeks and a comprehensive assessment no later than 12 weeks; earlier and more frequent care is needed for hypertension, diabetes, cesarean recovery, mood symptoms, feeding difficulty, substance use, or social risk. The plan should begin before discharge and state who manages blood pressure, glucose, wounds, mood screens, feeding, medications, and emergency concerns.

Primary care may see a patient before obstetric follow-up or after the patient has been lost to that system. Ask every recently pregnant patient when and how delivery occurred, gestational age, complications, procedures, transfusion, anesthesia, discharge medications, infant status, feeding plan, and scheduled follow-up.

Part 2 — Urgent Maternal Warning Signs

Pregnancy-related complications can occur during pregnancy and up to one year after delivery. Emergency warning signs include severe or worsening headache, visual change, seizure, chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, confusion, severe persistent abdominal pain, heavy bleeding, fever, unilateral limb swelling or pain, overwhelming weakness, and thoughts of harming self or baby. Always document recent pregnancy in the handoff so emergency clinicians consider pregnancy-related disease.

Listen when a patient says something is wrong. Normalizing every symptom as sleep deprivation can delay recognition of hemorrhage, infection, cardiomyopathy, pulmonary embolism, or severe depression.

Part 3 — Bleeding: Lochia Versus Hemorrhage

Lochia normally changes in amount and character over time, but heavy bleeding, soaking a pad in an hour, large clots, syncope, tachycardia, pallor, severe weakness, or increasing bleeding after it had been improving requires urgent assessment. Secondary postpartum hemorrhage can occur days to weeks later because of retained tissue, subinvolution, infection, or coagulation problems.

Do not rely on visible blood alone. Assess perfusion, orthostatic symptoms when safe, abdominal or uterine pain, fever, discharge odor, medications, and anemia symptoms. Instability requires emergency transport and hemorrhage-capable care.

Part 4 — Hypertension and Cardiopulmonary Disease

Preeclampsia may first present postpartum. Persistent severe headache, visual symptoms, right-upper-quadrant or epigastric pain, severe blood pressure, dyspnea, or seizure requires emergency evaluation. Peripartum cardiomyopathy may present with progressive dyspnea, orthopnea, edema, cough, chest symptoms, palpitations, or profound fatigue. These findings can be mistaken for normal postpartum changes.

Sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, hemoptysis, syncope, hypoxemia, or unilateral leg swelling raises concern for venous thromboembolism. Do not use a normal appearance or young age to reassure a high-risk patient.

Part 5 — Infection and Wound Assessment

Fever, uterine tenderness, foul-smelling lochia, or systemic illness can indicate endometritis. Inspect cesarean or perineal wounds when relevant for separation, drainage, erythema, warmth, disproportionate pain, or necrosis. Urinary symptoms, retention, pyelonephritis, mastitis, respiratory infection, and sepsis remain in the differential.

Severe pain out of proportion, rapidly spreading erythema, crepitus, hypotension, altered mental status, or toxicity requires emergency surgical-capable evaluation. A portal photograph cannot safely rule out deep infection.

Part 6 — Mental Health and Safety

Differentiate transient early emotional lability from persistent depression, anxiety, trauma symptoms, obsessive intrusive thoughts, mania, psychosis, and suicidal or infanticidal risk. Use a validated perinatal mental-health screen within a system that can assess and respond to positive results. Ask directly about self-harm, harm to the infant, hallucinations, delusions, severe insomnia without fatigue, disorganization, and ability to perform essential care.

Postpartum psychosis is an emergency. Mania, hallucinations, paranoia, bizarre beliefs, severe confusion, or thoughts of harming self or baby require immediate psychiatric and emergency support; the patient and infant should not be left without a safe responsible adult. Also assess intimate partner violence, reproductive coercion, food and housing insecurity, and substance use.

Part 7 — Recovery, Pelvic Floor, and Sexual Health

Assess pain, incision or laceration healing, bowel and bladder function, urinary or fecal incontinence, retention, constipation, hemorrhoids, pelvic pressure, and mobility. Pelvic-floor therapy, urogynecology, colorectal, or surgical referral may be appropriate for persistent dysfunction, prolapse, severe laceration consequences, or pain.

Discuss sexual activity without assumptions. Pain, dryness, trauma, fatigue, body changes, relationship context, and lactational hypoestrogenism may contribute. Provide consent-centered counseling, lubricant or other appropriate support, and evaluation for infection, wound problems, or pelvic pathology when symptoms persist.

Part 8 — Contraception and Reproductive Planning

Ovulation can precede the first postpartum menses, and breastfeeding does not reliably prevent pregnancy unless strict lactational amenorrhea criteria are met. Review pregnancy goals, method preference, blood pressure, VTE risk, lactation, medication interactions, and timing. Use current U.S. MEC/SPR rather than assuming every estrogen-containing method is appropriate immediately postpartum.

Part 9 — Chronic Disease Transition

Pregnancy complications forecast later health. Preeclampsia and other hypertensive disorders increase cardiovascular risk. GDM increases type 2 diabetes risk. Preterm birth may identify maternal vascular or inflammatory risk. Reconcile antihypertensives and diabetes medicines, schedule postpartum glucose testing, assess renal and thyroid needs, update vaccines, and connect the patient to ongoing primary care.

Medication decisions during lactation should use current, drug-specific evidence such as LactMed and infant age/health—not a blanket instruction to stop breastfeeding or stop essential treatment. Coordinate with pediatrics and obstetrics when exposure or infant risk is complex.

Part 10 — Equity and Access

Transportation, insurance loss, paid leave, language, childcare, sleep, racism, immigration concerns, and fragmented records can block postpartum care. Offer telehealth when clinically appropriate, combine visits, arrange home pressure monitoring, use interpreters, simplify scheduling, and identify a named care coordinator. Missed visits are a signal to redesign access, not proof that the patient does not value health.

Clinical Case 1 — Heavy Bleeding at Home

Two weeks postpartum, a patient reports suddenly soaking pads, passing large clots, and feeling faint. The FNP arranges emergency transport and communicates possible secondary hemorrhage; routine office evaluation is unsafe.

Clinical Case 2 — Breathlessness Labeled as Fatigue

Six weeks postpartum, a patient has worsening orthopnea, tachycardia, edema, and cannot walk across the room without dyspnea. The FNP considers cardiomyopathy and thromboembolism and directs emergency cardiopulmonary assessment rather than advising more rest.

Clinical Case 3 — No Sleep and Paranoia

Eight days postpartum, a patient has not slept, is increasingly disorganized, hears a voice, and believes the baby is possessed. The FNP recognizes postpartum psychosis, keeps the patient and infant with safe supervision, and activates emergency psychiatric care.

FNP High-Yield Framework: FOURTH

  1. F — Find danger first: bleeding, pressure, brain, breathing, clot, fever, pain, and psychiatric safety.
  2. O — Obstetric history: delivery, complications, procedures, medications, infant, and follow-up.
  3. U — Unify recovery: wound, pelvic floor, mood, feeding, sleep, sexuality, and social support.
  4. R — Reconcile risk: hypertension, diabetes, VTE, medication, lactation, and future pregnancy.
  5. T — Transition care: primary care, specialists, testing, vaccines, and result ownership.
  6. H — Hear the patient: respect concerns, remove access barriers, and use explicit return precautions.

Take-Home Summary

Postpartum care is longitudinal, multidisciplinary, and inseparable from primary care. FNP-level practice recognizes emergency warning signs, assesses physical and mental recovery together, supports feeding and reproductive goals, and converts pregnancy complications into a prevention and follow-up plan that lasts beyond the fourth trimester.

Educational note: This lesson does not replace ACOG/CDC guidance, local postpartum protocols, psychiatric emergency procedures, or individualized care. Heavy bleeding, seizure, severe headache or visual change, chest pain, dyspnea, syncope, unilateral limb swelling, fever with systemic illness, severe abdominal pain, confusion, psychosis, or thoughts of harm requires immediate evaluation.
